abstract:
COMP360, a form of synthetic psilocybin (PSY), is being developed for the treatment of treatment-resistant depression (TRD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Orally-administered PSY is rapidly cleaved to the active moiety, psilocin (PSI), which undergoes further metabolism to psilocin-O-glucuronide (PSIG) and 4-hydroxyindole-3-acetic acid (4-HIAA).

Methods for the quantification of PSY and its metabolites in plasma (PSY - 0.5 to 500 ng/mL; PSI - 0.5 to 200 ng/mL; PSIG - 1.0 to 400 ng/mL; 4-HIAA - 5 to 2000 ng/mL), and PSI in human urine (0.5 to 200 ng/mL), were developed and validated across 2 vendor bioanalytical laboratories. Plasma samples were processed by simple protein precipitation, and the extracts evaporated to dryness and reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid in water. Chromatographic separation of analytes from endogenous components, and from one another, was effected using a Waters HSS T3 analytical column and detection was performed using tandem mass spectrometry.

Method validation was conducted, and met acceptance criteria, according to ICH M10 guidance. Appropriate reference standards were sourced for each analyte and stable isotopically-labelled versions of each analyte were used as internal standards. Suitable conditions for sample handling and storage were assessed, and acceptable stability results were validated. Stability conditions were limited by the facile oxidation of psilocin but plasma samples could be kept thawed on wet ice for 8h or frozen at -80{degrees}C for 6 months, and subjected to 4 freeze/thaw cycles. The validated ranges were shown to be appropriate for the concentrations determined in samples taken in subsequent clinical studies, and data reliability was demonstrated from successful ISR analysis. Comparative performance of the multi-analyte method, across vendor laboratories, was shown through conduct of a cross-validation study employing spiked-QC and incurred samples.
